title: Federal Appeals Court Slams DOJ Emergency Attempt to Separate California Ballots
snippet: A 9th Circuit panel ruled 2-1 against the Justice Department's last-minute push to force California election officials to segregate 20,000 mail-in ballots.
content:
A federal appeals court has shut down an emergency bid by the Justice Department to force California to separate roughly 20,000 mail-in ballots cast by alleged noncitizens, chiding federal officials for creating a "self-constructed" crisis.

In a 2-1 ruling issued late Monday, a panel for the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals held that the DOJ improperly bypassed a lower-court judge who was already scheduled to hear arguments on the emergency request.

A Fractured Panel Scolds DOJ's Rush

The majority opinion combined the votes of Judge Mark Bennett, an appointee of former President Donald Trump, and Judge Gabriel Sanchez, an appointee of President Joe Biden. In a concurrence, Bennett sharply criticized the government's arguments, writing that the Justice Department offered "no workable plan of any kind" to segregate the ballots without triggering "catastrophic consequences" for California's ongoing election.

Dissenting from the ruling, Trump-appointed Judge Patrick Bumatay contended that federal laws barring noncitizens from voting should supersede state administrative procedures. Bumatay argued that every day the court delays intervention increases the risk of illegal votes diluting valid ones in the upcoming midterms.

Newsom Reacts as Hearing Moves Back to District Court

California Governor Gavin Newsom praised the appellate ruling, framing the DOJ's lawsuit as an authoritarian power grab. "Trump is illegally trying to seize powers in the Constitution entrusted to others so he can stay in power," Newsom said in a public statement.

The procedural decision sends the case back to U.S. District Judge David Carter in Los Angeles for a scheduled Tuesday afternoon hearing. Depending on the outcome in district court, the Justice Department could still launch a new round of emergency appeals, potentially taking the legal battle to the U.S. Supreme Court.
